episode_thesis: Baltas and Kaastrup-Larsen argue that the April 2025 V-shape hurt trend followers of every speed because turning points cannot be predicted, so what matters is leverage going into them; Baltas floats a dynamic (lower when signal-to-noise is poor) volatility target while admitting it is hard to implement without hindsight bias. Both conclude that trend following should be held as a strategic, never-timed allocation (insurance-like), that institutional constraints explain much of what alternatives earn, and that systematic managers should neither react emotionally to a bad run nor be dogmatic about their models.

speakers.name: Nick Baltas
speakers.role: Systematic investor and academic-minded quant (runs systematic strategies; guest co-host of the Systematic Investor series)

worldview_premises.premise: A V-shape is two reversals in a row; any trend follower is hit on both legs, and no speed of trend signal avoids it (slow ones ride the whole V, fast ones lose less going down but recover less).
worldview_premises.support: Logic of how trend signals work, illustrated with April 2025 and earlier V-events (SVB, Aug 2024).

worldview_premises.premise: Turning points are not predictable, so the controllable variable is how much leverage the book carries when one arrives (twice the leverage, roughly twice the loss).
worldview_premises.support: Arithmetic of leverage; no empirical test offered.

worldview_premises.premise: Realized portfolio volatility is a function of leverage, which in turn depends on diversification and correlation; when positions are mixed (low trend barometer) more leverage is needed to hit a fixed vol target, when directional (high barometer) the risk is concentrated in equity or rate beta.
worldview_premises.support: Portfolio mechanics from his own trend barometer.

worldview_premises.premise: Investors are loss-averse (prospect theory), so being under-levered during a drawdown is a rational preference even at the cost of upside, which is the motive for dynamic volatility targets.
worldview_premises.support: Economic theory and social experiments (cited generally, no specific study).

worldview_premises.premise: Trend strength does not predict subsequent trend performance, except that very high trendiness precedes underperformance because the many trends reduce to few correlated principal components.
worldview_premises.support: Historical look at his barometer versus subsequent performance; no figures given.

worldview_premises.premise: Past performance is only a weak predictor of future returns, and trend-following outperformance often begins after a stretch of underperformance, so timing allocations in and out of trend is not feasible; it should be a strategic, insurance-like allocation.
worldview_premises.support: Cites analyses by Katy Kaminski and Man Group, plus an insurance analogy.

worldview_premises.premise: Many anomalies and the returns of alternatives come from structural constraints (leverage limits, benchmarking, capacity) rather than behavioural bias; so relaxing the constraints would change the returns.
Mean-variance logic (100% managed futures) is incomplete because allocators are judged relative to a benchmark, so career and tracking-error risk set the real allocation.
worldview_premises.support: Earlier conversations with the host; his experience with institutions.

worldview_premises.premise: New alternative/ML data and LLM tools are powerful but their alpha value and decay mechanism must be tested, and LLM output must be verified.
worldview_premises.support: Personal anecdote: an LLM fabricated ten references to an academic paper.

worldview_premises.premise: Information shocks like the April 2025 tariff pause cannot be foreseen or captured by systematic signals; at such times signals are mostly noise.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why V-shaped markets hurt trend followers and what leverage does to the loss

steps.from: Market falls then rebounds sharply (April 2025, Aug 2024, SVB)
steps.to: Trend signals reverse after the first leg and again on the rebound
steps.why: A V is two reversions back to back.

steps.from: Positions were wrongly set in every asset class at once (oil, rates, dollar, equities)
steps.to: No offsetting sector cushions the loss
steps.why: Directional bets across the book were all against the turn.

steps.from: Faster signals
steps.to: Lose less on the way down but recover less; slower signals ride the whole V
steps.why: Different trajectories, similar end result; all are negative.

steps.from: Turning point unpredictable
steps.to: Loss scales with leverage entering it
steps.why: Twice the leverage doubles the loss.

mechanism_chains.evidence: April 2025 trend results (BTOP50 -3.39%, SG CTA -7.6%, SG Trend -10.4% YTD at mid-June 2025); no formal study.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: If V-shapes were not more frequent, lowering leverage would just give up trend payoffs (own hindsight caveat).

mechanism_chains.topic: Dynamic volatility target as a response to more frequent V-shapes

steps.from: Realized vol is tied to leverage, itself a function of correlation and how directional positions are
steps.to: A fixed vol target implies leverage that moves with diversification
steps.why: Mixed signals need higher leverage to hit the same target.

steps.from: V-shapes more frequent and signal-to-noise low
steps.to: Lower vol targets and less leverage may be warranted
steps.why: Limits turning-point loss.

steps.from: Loss aversion
steps.to: Preference for being under-levered in drawdown
steps.why: A dollar lost hurts more than a dollar gained helps.

steps.from: Cutting leverage after losses
steps.to: Looks good on recent episodes through hindsight but backtests would show cases where missing emerging trends hurt
steps.why: It is a trade-off, plus path dependency and an ambiguous benchmark (reduced book versus the full-risk book).

steps.from: Aggregate trendiness as a signal to scale
steps.to: Does not work historically
steps.why: No link to subsequent performance, except very high trendiness precedes weakness.

mechanism_chains.evidence: SG Trend index realized vol of about 7-11% in the last 1-2 years versus 10-13% historically, read as managers already running lower or more dynamic risk; otherwise conversation with investors and theory.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: When the rule is fitted to the last drawdown or when trends are strong and it reduces exposure to emerging ones.

mechanism_chains.topic: Constraints create anomalies (low beta) and make alternatives' paper returns unreplicable at scale

steps.from: Leverage-constrained investors cannot lever a 1% vol asset 10x
steps.to: They bid up higher-vol, higher-beta assets
steps.why: Sharpe-equivalent assets are not accessible equivalents.

steps.from: Benchmarked investors minimise tracking error
steps.to: Demand concentrates in beta-one assets, so high beta underperforms
steps.why: Equilibrium pricing.

steps.from: Alternatives are held in small amounts due to governance limits
steps.to: Their historical returns may reflect that scarcity
steps.why: More inflows would hit capacity and lower returns; circular.

steps.from: Allocators judged versus 60/40
steps.to: Optimal mean-variance weight (100% managed futures) is not the practical weight
steps.why: Career and tracking-error risk.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Academic equilibrium arguments; no data in the episode.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; Baltas notes pure substitution will not perform as on paper because the circle closes.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why trend should be held strategically and not timed

steps.from: Trend followers' role is to diversify policy portfolios in prolonged corrections
steps.to: It is statistical insurance and cannot be timed
steps.why: You do not buy car insurance after the crash.

steps.from: Past performance weakly predicts future returns; outperformance often starts after underperformance
steps.to: Exiting after losses is the worst decision
steps.why: Kaminski and Man Group analyses.

steps.from: Trend has no positive daily skew, only over longer windows
steps.to: Judging it day to day is unfair; organisational discipline and expectations matter
steps.why: Return pattern is longer-window.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Cited third-party analyses (Kaminski, Man Group) plus the host's late-November 2021 anecdote.

decision_process.practice: Uses a trend barometer (reading 39 in June 2025) to gauge how strong and directional the trend signals are; not used as a timing predictor.
decision_process.why: Describes the portfolio but historically does not predict returns.

decision_process.practice: Adds carry and mean-reversion components to trend; in 2025 these diversified trend exposures without lowering the correlation profile to the benchmark.
decision_process.why: Diversifies trend risk in noisy markets.

decision_process.practice: Trend portfolio built from signals plus a risk model (vol and correlation estimates), with portfolio vol either targeted or bounded so investors can scale it next to 60/40; dynamic risk scaling across markets is accepted.
Considers a time-varying portfolio vol target (lower when signal-to-noise is low); no specific rule offered.
decision_process.why: Limit leverage into unpredictable turning points and manage the pain of losses at the margin, without going in or out of the strategy.

decision_process.practice: Tolerates the known losing regime rather than altering the models: most trend investors did not change models after the V-shape.
decision_process.why: The sign of the V-shape effect is understood; only the size is open.

decision_process.practice: Tests new data vendors for alpha value and decay mechanism, verifies LLM outputs, and asks the team to test more of the new data.
decision_process.why: Many vendors pitch ML sentiment/alpha claims; LLMs fabricated references.

decision_process.practice: Treats trend as a strategic allocation sized appropriately and left alone.

speakers.evidence_style: First-principles and academic-literature reasoning (prospect theory, structural-constraint equilibrium), his own barometer and index statistics, and cited third-party analyses; openly flags hindsight bias in any recent-drawdown rule.

current_views.view: April 2025 was another V-shape; trend followers were hit twice, with every asset class wrongly positioned.
Trend remains a crisis hedge and investors stay because no sustained crisis has occurred; no outflows and rising inflows.
current_views.reasoning: The scenario that justifies the strategy has not occurred.

current_views.view: Trend index and managers are weak YTD (BTOP50 -3.39%, SG CTA -7.6%, SG Trend -10.4%, short-term traders -3.32%); trend barometer 39, weak but stable.

Systematic macro reading for 2025: falling growth with range-bound yields and inflation pointed to being out of equities, long gold or a steepener; fast systematic signals were less responsive to these themes.
current_views.reasoning: Macro dynamics versus noisy fast signals.

current_views.view: Do not react emotionally or abandon the models, but do not be dogmatic: the market is evolving.
current_views.reasoning: Not enough yet learnt; question whether more discretion is needed is legitimate but not the answer.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host of Top Traders Unplugged; veteran hedge fund (trend following) manager
speakers.speaker_note: Takes positions mainly as the host's comments; the June 2025 performance review (MT087-C04-1, corrected from Baltas) is his. Claims about his firm ('we') refer to his own CTA business.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend followers are not all alike; the 12-14 months after 2024 exposed differences in risk budgeting and design among managers that look correlated in normal times.
Dynamic risk budgeting using vol and correlations beyond price is valuable (his firm has used it for over 12 years), though critics call it contrary to pure trend following.
Trend timing is not possible: even a very large one-day CTA loss (late November 2021) preceded a very strong 2022, and long losing runs can be followed by a great month.
Constraints on institutions are rarely set for investors' benefit, and indebted governments could in future dictate pension holdings to place their debt.
worldview_premises.support: Speculation, flagged by him as such.

worldview_premises.premise: Rejecting some data and technology innovations is as important as adopting the right ones.
Asness: the 'missing the 10 best days' sales argument is misleading because investors who miss best days would also miss some worst days.
worldview_premises.support: Paper by Cliff Asness (cited, not detailed).

disagreements.topic: Whether to cut leverage dynamically versus not reacting to the path

positions.speaker: Nick Baltas
positions.position: Open to a dynamic (lower) vol target when signal-to-noise is low, but sees hindsight and path-dependency problems and no good predictor.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen

disagreements.topic: Static versus dynamic sizing and the extent of timing

positions.speaker: Nick Baltas
positions.position: Trend is a strategic allocation that cannot be timed, yet moderating risk through vol scaling is a different, marginal tool.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The tension between 'trend cannot be timed' and the proposal for dynamic vol targets is acknowledged by Baltas but only resolved by distinguishing exposure moderation from in-or-out timing; no testable rule is given.
Realised vol of the SG Trend index being 7-11% versus 10-13% historically is flagged by Baltas himself as heavy averaging, so it is weak evidence for managers lowering risk.
Claim that V-shapes are more frequent rests on three events (SVB, Aug 2024, April 2025), with the regime-change question left open.
No numbers behind the claims that trendiness does not predict performance or that Kaminski/Man Group analyses show outperformance after underperformance; both are cited from memory.
The speculation about governments dictating pension holdings is explicitly labeled as speculation.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Observables the speakers say matter: the frequency of V-shaped reversals and the signal-to-noise of markets (for leverage), the level of the trend barometer (very high precedes weakness, otherwise uninformative), realized vol of trend indices, and whether a sustained crisis occurs (the scenario for which trend is held). No price forecast is given; horizon is strategic, years.
reader_inferences: (reader) Baltas's lower-vol-target idea is a bet that shorter, noisier information cycles raise the share of turning-point losses; if V-shapes are random, it only cuts return.
(reader) The structural-constraints argument implies that alternatives' historical premia may shrink as allocations grow.

(reader) The advice to hold trend as a never-timed 10% allocation conflicts with the idea of trading the vol target off recent drawdown, unless the target moves on ex-ante signal-to-noise rather than realized losses.
